country: United States (North Carolina, 100 counties; 91 in balanced panel)
design: panel FE (county-month; county, year, month FE plus county linear trends; falsification test on late-pregnancy job losses)
shock: County-level monthly job losses from business closings and layoffs, as % of working-age (25-64) population
fertility_outcome: county-month birth rate of 15-19 year-olds (annualized, indexed by conception month), by race
estimate: Black teens: job loss to 1% of working-age pop reduces births by 1.15 per 1,000 (job loss 0-4 months post-conception) and 1.74 per 1,000 (1-9 months pre-conception), i.e. 1.6%-2.4% (abstract: ~2%). White teens: little/no effect. Women 20-24: no significant effect.
units: births per 1,000 teens (annualized) per 1 pp job loss
identifies_substitution_effect: no - a county-level labor demand shock hits teens' families' income, parental/own job prospects, expectations and sexual/contraceptive behavior; teens are not the wage-earning mothers, and no female-specific wage or non-labor-income-held-constant variation is used.
routes_to: Not C.2.e: mostly C.1.a (income/economic-resource shock via family job loss) plus expectations/uncertainty; teen margins (abortion, contraception, sexual activity) rather than maternal opportunity cost of time. Not REVERSE (job loss is exogenous to fertility). Recommend exclude from C.2.e or retain as background only.
sample_n: 20,475 county-months (91 counties); 231,712 teen births Jan 1990-Jun 2010 (white and black teens)

period: 1990-2014 (stacked decadal first differences 1990-2000, 2000-2014; fertility outcome through 2016)
design: IV (shift-share/Bartik): China import-penetration exposure instrumented by Chinese imports to 8 other high-income countries; stacked first differences, state-clustered SEs, weighted by CZ population
shock: China import-competition shock to local manufacturing, apportioned into male-intensive and female-intensive industry components (unit shock ~ average decadal CZ rise in exposure)
fertility_outcome: Births per 1,000 women ages 18-39 (Table 3 col B4); also % women married, % women with children, % mothers unmarried
estimate: Overall unit trade shock: -2.02 births per 1,000 women 18-39 (1990 mean level 86.87). Female-industry-intensive shock: +2.51 births per 1,000 (SE 1.25, p<=0.05). Male-industry-intensive shock: -6.10 births per 1,000 (SE 1.28, p<=0.01).
units: births per 1,000 women ages 18-39 per unit shock
elasticity: null (no wage elasticity reported; female-industry shock reduces female manufacturing employment by 2.56 pp and relative female earnings, but no earnings-to-fertility elasticity is estimated; the +2.51 is a reduced form on an employment/exposure shock, not a per-wage elasticity)
routes_to: Primary headline (overall shock reducing fertility via male stature/marriage-market) routes OUT of C.2.e to C.1.a (male income / marriage-market value). Only the gender-disaggregated female-industry coefficient (+2.51 births/1,000: adverse shock to female-intensive employment raises fertility) is C.2.e-relevant, as partial/suggestive evidence of a female price-of-time channel; it also lowers female household income so the income effect is not netted out, and it is a secondary estimate collinear (rho=0.80) with the male component.

study: Kotsadam-Pieters-Villanger 2025 (G2LM|LIC Policy Brief 84; Ethiopia factory-job RCT)
country: Ethiopia (27 garment and shoe factories, five industrializing regions)
period: 9-year follow-up from baseline (calendar years not stated in the brief)
shock: Randomized offer of a formal factory wage job to married women who had applied to factories
fertility_outcome: total number of births / children; probability of becoming a mother among baseline-childless women; time-to-birth (Kaplan-Meier)
estimate: about +5% in total births (long run); +15 percentage points in probability of becoming a mother among women childless at baseline
units: percent change in births; percentage points
identifies_substitution_effect: partial - randomized job access isolates the causal effect of wage employment, but it bundles the substitution effect with a large income/savings effect; the brief says the long-run income effect outweighed the short-run time-cost effect, and no birth divergence appeared in years 1-3 while employment gaps were largest (postponement only).
routes_to: C.2.e (opportunity-cost channel, only as a short-run postponement) with strong C.1.a (income effect) overlap; NOT reverse-causality/selection because the job offer is randomized. Net effect of wage employment is wrong-signed for the substitution hypothesis.

country: Germany (West and East; German Socio-Economic Panel). NOTE: Germany, not Italy.
shock: Industry-level import competition and export opportunities in trade with Eastern Europe (China secondary), assigned by individual's initial industry; instrumented with other high-income countries' trade with the East; individual, year x state, year x occupation, 1-digit industry FE
fertility_outcome: Probability of a birth in the year (individuals aged 20-44); also first child, marital/nonmarital fertility, completed fertility (number of children), marriage, divorce, cohabitation
estimate: Import exposure coefficient -0.120 on birth probability (pooled); text: average 1991-2018 import increase lowers birth probability by 1.6 pp (men -1.8 pp). Export exposure +0.061; average export increase +1.1 pp. Women only: import -0.078, export +0.043 (both insignificant).
units: coefficient on 0/1 birth indicator per unit of exposure (2SLS); pp for average exposure change
se: Pooled import SE 0.046 (p<0.05); pooled export SE 0.033 (p<0.10); female import SE 0.081, female export SE 0.055; clustered at industry level
elasticity: Not reported. Mean birth probability 0.042 pooled (0.030 women), so -1.6 pp is roughly -38% relative to the mean, my derived figure rather than a paper statistic. Completed fertility (Table 4, pooled): import -0.471 (SE 0.223), export +0.614 (SE 0.172); women import -0.295 (0.282).
identifies_substitution_effect: no — the shock lowers (import) or raises (export) labor demand mainly for low-educated men (male import effect on income -0.436***, women +0.087 SE 0.356, ns), so fertility moves with income/job security (children as normal goods), which is the opposite sign from a rising female price of time.
routes_to: C.1.a (income / labor-demand effect, normal-good sign) and the male-labor-market/uncertainty channel; NOT C.2.e. Female-specific estimates are null and women's wage/employment were not significantly affected, so no price-of-time test.
sample_n: About 55,000 person-years from about 6,500 individuals; fertility regressions 51,664 pooled (25,463 women, 26,181 men); completed fertility 10,482 (5,532 women)

period: Register data 1988-2004; base years (plant closures) 1991-93; followed 3-4 yrs pre to 11 yrs post
design: event-study / panel (displaced vs non-displaced couples, plant-closure displacement, OLS with rich pre-displacement controls)
shock: Job loss from plant closure (also mass-layoff robustness) of the woman, or of her spouse, in couples where woman aged 20-40
fertility_outcome: cumulative number of children (completed-fertility proxy at 11 yrs post) and annual birth indicator
estimate: -0.03 children per displaced woman by ~year 11 (published abstract: 3 fewer children per 100 displaced females; IZA WP 6707 version says ~4 per 100, -0.04). Highly educated women: ~5 fewer per 100. Male job loss: no significant effect.
units: children per woman (cumulative number of children)
identifies_substitution_effect: no - plant closure moves the woman's earnings and employment (and career continuity) and also household income together; authors explicitly attribute the effect to career-break/human-capital concerns, not to a lower price of time, and the predicted substitution effect (cheaper time -> more fertility) has the OPPOSITE sign to the observed negative effect.
routes_to: C.2.e as an adjacent/contrary-signed test (displacement is a drop in female wage/employment, and fertility FALLS, i.e. inconsistent with a pure substitution-effect reading); also informs C.1.a (male job loss, a larger family-income drop, has no effect, suggesting weak income effect) and a career-interruption/uncertainty channel (not cleanly C.2.e). Not REVERSE.
sample_n: Table 1 (published): females 7,011 displaced / 249,894 non-displaced; males 11,143 displaced / 373,588 non-displaced

period: 1983-2003 (fertility histories reconstructed retrospectively from 2003 ISTAT-LFS; wage equations from BOI-SHIW 1991-2002)
design: panel FE - no; discrete-time logit hazard models (event history) with generated regressor (predicted wage), bootstrapped SEs; OLS cross-section wage equation (Tobit) in first stage
shock: Predicted hourly wage (potential female wage / opportunity cost) imputed to ISTAT-LFS women from BOI-SHIW earnings equations based on education and other characteristics; time-varying
fertility_outcome: Discrete-time hazard of first, second and third birth (timing / parity progression)
estimate: First birth, general wage effect: Wage coefficient -0.344, (Wage)^2 +0.066 (Table 2 col 1); wage x age interactions strongly negative at young ages (-0.759 at 15-17; -0.292 at 27-29) and turning positive after ~34 (+0.078 at 34-35, +0.123 at 36-40, Table 2 col 3). Second birth: Wage -0.071, Wage^2 +0.052 (Table 3). Third birth: Wage -0.03 (ns), Wage^2 +0.098.
units: logit hazard coefficients (wage units = predicted hourly wage; scaling not stated in text)
se: First birth Wage SE 0.006, Wage^2 SE 0.003; second birth Wage SE 0.009; third birth Wage SE 0.018 (bootstrap, 300 reps)
identifies_substitution_effect: no - predicted wage is a function of observed education/characteristics (so it proxies schooling/socioeconomic status), husband's income/wage is not controlled (no partner data), so non-labor/household income is not held constant; effect is mainly postponement with partial recuperation, not a clean price-of-time substitution effect.
routes_to: C.2.e (descriptive/associational support for timing delay); partly overlaps D.2.a (education/returns to schooling) because wage is imputed from education; no reverse-causality fix
sample_n: 34,129 women; 425,014 person-period obs; 25,233 first-birth spells (second birth: 25,227 women, 122,608 obs; third birth: 14,483 women, 83,949 obs). Wage equation sample: 20,003 individuals / 4,749 women in childbearing stage in BOI-SHIW 2002

design: DiD (state and quarter-year FE, state covariates, state-specific nonlinear quarter-year trends)
shock: State minimum wage increases ($1 increase), per abstract
fertility_outcome: Adolescent birth rate (vital statistics, quarterly state level)
estimate: A $1 increase in minimum wage reduces adolescent birth rates by about 2% (abstract only); implies roughly 5,000 fewer adolescent births annually nationwide
units: % change in adolescent birth rate per $1 minimum wage
identifies_substitution_effect: no - retrieval failed for full text; per abstract only: minimum wage raises both price of low-wage time and household income (and affects adolescents mainly via family/parental income and local labor market), so it does not isolate the female substitution channel.
routes_to: Tentative: weak C.2.e / possibly C.1.a (income) or other; adolescents' own wage is not clearly the relevant margin. Needs confirmation on full read.

design: panel / discrete-time hazard (logit) on register data; descriptive correlation, not causal (author states estimates are non-causal)
shock: Lagged annual own earnings quintile (relative to same sex and age cohort-year), Q1 reference
fertility_outcome: Yearly first-birth probability (odds ratio from hazard model)
estimate: Women, pooled Model 1b, odds of first birth vs lowest earnings quintile: Q2 1.24, Q3 1.67, Q4 2.18, Q5 2.50. Men: Q2 1.47, Q3 1.92, Q4 2.31, Q5 2.67. Female correlation strengthens over 1995-2010 (Q5 OR roughly 1.8 in 1995 to roughly 3.6 in 2010, read from Figure 1b); men's rises less (Q5 about 2.3 to 3.5, Figure 1a).
identifies_substitution_effect: no - women's earnings are positively associated with first births, so the income/timing/career-maturity channels dominate; this contradicts a net substitution effect, and the descriptive design does not isolate the price of time.
routes_to: C.2.e as contrary or null evidence; also bears on C.1.a (income effect) and REVERSE (career maturity and partnership selection). Author notes the correlation turned more positive for women as childcare expanded, i.e. substitution weakens when work-family compatibility rises.
sample_n: Women 3,267,393 person-years (270,137 first births); men 4,777,842 person-years (287,030 first births)

design: structural (general-equilibrium OLG model with endogenous fertility and human capital, calibrated, plus descriptive time-series facts using HP-filtered cyclical components)
shock: Gender-specific employment/income volatility (men concentrated in procyclical industries, women in countercyclical ones) and rising women's relative income (breadwinner status); counterfactual swaps of gender-industry allocation
fertility_outcome: Cyclicality of fertility (correlation of cyclical component of quarterly fertility rate with GDP); level of fertility and child human capital in counterfactuals
estimate: Correlation of fertility with GDP cycle: -0.334 (1960-1974) vs +0.547 (1975-2018). Model: change in gender employment cyclicality explains 38-44% of emergence of procyclical fertility; lower relative income alone explains 56-62%. Counterfactual (men in countercyclical, women in procyclical industries): fertility +0.12% and countercyclical, human capital/quality 0.20% lower; 'women-nurse' economy: fertility 0.15% lower, human capital 0.25% higher.
units: correlation coefficients; % of change in cyclicality explained; % level changes in counterfactuals
elasticity: null (no fertility elasticity to female wage reported; paper states in benchmark 1975-2018 calibration the income effect of women's income slightly dominates the substitution effect, so a rise in women's income slightly raises fertility)
routes_to: Weak/contextual for C.2.e: it is a macro cyclicality model, not a causal estimate of the female wage substitution effect. Time-cost (substitution) vs income effects are modelled but calibrated, not identified; benchmark finds income effect slightly dominating for women. Better treated as theory/context for C.2.e and business-cycle fertility (cyclical income, not secular female wage rise).
sample_n: US aggregate quarterly time series, ~58 years (no micro sample); model calibrated to moments (not an estimation sample N)

country: Germany, France, Italy, UK, Czechia, Poland (NUTS-2 regions)
design: panel FE with shift-share IV (2SLS), instrumenting industry robot stock with other countries' stocks; separate models by country
shock: Regional exposure to industrial robots (IFR robot stock weighted by regional industry employment structure)
fertility_outcome: Regional TFR and age-specific fertility rates (20-24 ... 45+)
estimate: Basic 2SLS exposure coefficient on TFR: Germany -0.00016 (ns); France +0.00003 (ns); Italy -0.00118 (p<0.10); UK +0.00168 (ns); Czechia&Poland +0.00053 (ns). Germany 35-39 ASFR -0.00011***, 40-44 -0.00005***; Italy 25-29 -0.00090***. No sex-specific estimate (regional aggregate).
units: coefficient (TFR points per unit robot exposure)
se: SEs clustered by region; main-text tables report only significance stars (SEs only in appendix Tables 8-12, not extracted)
identifies_substitution_effect: no - robot exposure is a labor-demand/job-insecurity shock to both sexes, not the female price of time; fertility effects are not separated into substitution vs income effects.
routes_to: Weak/indirect C.2.e at best; closer to labor-market-insecurity / income-shock channel (C.1.a-type). Authors' H2 (female-share-of-manufacturing moderator) not supported in DE/FR/IT (more negative where women's manufacturing share was larger; mixed, positive moderator in UK and CZ/PL).
sample_n: N=680 Germany (34 regions), 440 France (22), 400 Italy (20), 700 UK (35), 240 Czechia+Poland; 20 years

study: Van den Broeck & Maertens 2014 (Senegal horticultural export sector)

country: England / NW Europe (comparison: China, Southern and Eastern Europe)
period: Post-Black Death c.1350 to c.1750 (decline of EMP after 1750)
shock: Black Death mortality shock raising land-labor ratio, shifting agriculture toward pastoral production and raising the relative wage of female labor in horn (pastoral) vs grain
fertility_outcome: Births per peasant household (model-implied); female age at marriage / celibacy (descriptive); EMP avoided up to 1/3 of births (calibration)
estimate: Calibrated: EMP cuts births from pi=3 to b_min=2 per household (about -1/3 of births); peasant income about +20% (model) to +30% (constant-elasticity variant) above pre-plague level. Not an estimated effect.
units: model-implied % change in births / income (calibration, not regression)
elasticity: Calibration inputs only: birth-income elasticity 0 before EMP, 1.41 after (taken from Kelly 2005); death-rate elasticity -0.55 (Kelly 2005); women's grain productivity rho=0.5. No female-wage elasticity of fertility is estimated.
identifies_substitution_effect: no — it is a calibrated Malthusian model with no estimated treatment effect, and its own Prop. 2 says EMP emerges only when a subsistence (income) effect dominates the relative-wage (substitution) effect near subsistence, so the mechanism is not a clean price-of-time effect.
routes_to: C.2.e as a PRE-MODERN theory/mechanism and calibration study (not empirical); flag that the effect also leans on the income/subsistence channel (C.1.a) and on institutional farm service (celibacy contracts, a marriage-market/institution channel). Possible D.2.a-type marriage-institution overlap.
sample_n: Not applicable (no estimation sample; historical aggregates and Kussmaul 1981 farm-service figures used descriptively)
